title: At the Royal Berkshire Hospital, a scan supported by Brainomix 360 Stroke identifies an 83-year-old woman's major stroke, and she leaves for thrombectomy in Oxford within 25 minutes
summary: A scan supported by Brainomix 360 Stroke identified Jean Hines's major stroke on arrival, and she was transferred in 25 minutes for successful thrombectomy and recovered well.
account: Jean Hines, 83, collapsed at home and was taken to the Royal Berkshire Hospital, Reading, England, on a weekend in August. National Health Service (NHS) England's December 2025 statement gives no year, so 2025 is inferred. A scan carried out immediately on arrival, supported by the Brainomix AI imaging tool, identified a major stroke needing urgent specialist treatment. Within 25 minutes of reaching the emergency department she was on her way by ambulance to the John Radcliffe Hospital, Oxford. There she had a successful mechanical thrombectomy. She describes a very good physical recovery with no serious disabilities. NHS England states the Brainomix 360 Stroke tool is used in over 70 hospitals. It associates the tool with a 64-minute door-in-door-out reduction at primary stroke centers. In January 2024 NICE allowed e-Stroke, the earlier name of the Brainomix software, to be used in the NHS while more evidence is gathered. NICE stated that it is unclear how much of the faster access to treatment comes from the software. In January 2026 researchers at the University of Rzeszow in Poland, with no tie to Brainomix, reported that the software found 83.5% of anterior large vessel occlusions in 109 past transfers, and they estimated a median saving of up to 30 minutes in door-in-door-out time.
purpose: Brainomix 360 Stroke is built to analyze stroke imaging and support rapid treatment and transfer decisions, including selection for thrombectomy. This is its intended function.

ratings.reason: An 83-year-old woman was transferred rapidly for thrombectomy of a major stroke, and she describes a very good physical recovery with no serious disabilities. The sources do not show how much of the speed came from the software.

NHS England associates the tool with a 64-minute reduction in door-in-door-out time at primary stroke centers. The Lancet Digital Health study reports that thrombectomy rates rose from 2.3% to 4.6% at the 26 hospitals that implemented the software.

ai_role.statement: The AI-supported scan read identified the major stroke immediately on arrival, enabling a 25-minute door-in-door-out. The treatment itself (thrombectomy) was delivered by the Oxford team. The stroke would very likely have been diagnosed without AI. So the AI's contribution is the speed of decision and transfer. The Lancet Digital Health study (which has Brainomix co-authors alongside NHS lead authors) supports that at population level.

The Lancet Digital Health 7(12):100927. Three Brainomix employees and the corresponding author (dual NHS/Brainomix affiliation) are among 21 authors; lead authors are NHS and University of Oxford.
evidence.title: Artificial intelligence imaging decision support for acute stroke treatment in England: a prospective observational study
evidence.quote: Stroke AI imaging software was associated with increased endovascular thrombectomy rates across the English NHS.

evidence.citation: Wiącek M, Koszarska K, Kotlińska A, et al., Artificial intelligence-based software to support mechanical thrombectomy transfer decision in low-volume primary stroke centers: a multicenter, retrospective study, Neurologia i Neurochirurgia Polska, 22 January 2026. The authors are neurologists and medical students at the University of Rzeszow in Poland who declare no funding and no competing interests; they ran Brainomix 360 on the scans of 109 past transfers and estimated how much time it could have saved, without observing the Reading case.
evidence.title: Artificial intelligence-based software to support mechanical thrombectomy transfer decision in low-volume primary stroke centers: a multicenter, retrospective study
evidence.quote: The median maximal potential reduction in door-in-door-out (DIDO) time was estimated at 30 min

evidence.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, Artificial intelligence (AI)-derived software to help clinical decision making in stroke, HealthTech guidance HTG708 (formerly DG57), 23 January 2024. NICE has no stake in the software; its committee allowed e-Stroke in the NHS while more evidence is generated and found that the effect of the software on access to treatment is unclear.
evidence.title: Artificial intelligence (AI)-derived software to help clinical decision making in stroke: 1 Recommendations
evidence.quote: Some studies on 3 technologies (e-Stroke, RapidAI and Viz) in clinical practice suggest that people had faster or greater access to treatment after using the software, but it is unclear to what extent this is an effect of the software.

evidence.citation: Mallon D, Fallon M, Blana E, et al., Real-world evaluation of Brainomix e-Stroke software, Stroke and Vascular Neurology, 22 December 2023. The authors are neuroradiologists and stroke doctors at University College London Hospitals, and the lead author declares consultancy fees from Brainomix for algorithm development; they tested the software on 551 unselected patients in London.
evidence.title: Real-world evaluation of Brainomix e-Stroke software
evidence.quote: The accuracy of e-CTA for large vessel occlusions was 91.5%.

Brainomix employees co-wrote the Lancet Digital Health study, and the lead author of the London evaluation declares consultancy fees from Brainomix. NICE and the University of Rzeszow team have no stake in the software.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: A scan supported by Brainomix 360 Stroke identified Jean Hines's major stroke on arrival, and she was transferred in 25 minutes for successful thrombectomy and recovered well.
fields.account: Jean Hines, 83, collapsed at home and was taken to the Royal Berkshire Hospital, Reading, England, on a weekend in August. National Health Service (NHS) England's December 2025 statement gives no year, so 2025 is inferred. A scan carried out immediately on arrival, supported by the Brainomix AI imaging tool, identified a major stroke needing urgent specialist treatment. Within 25 minutes of reaching the emergency department she was on her way by ambulance to the John Radcliffe Hospital, Oxford. There she had a successful mechanical thrombectomy. She describes a very good physical recovery with no serious disabilities. NHS England states the Brainomix 360 Stroke tool is used in over 70 hospitals. It associates the tool with a 64-minute door-in-door-out reduction at primary stroke centers. In January 2024 NICE allowed e-Stroke, the earlier name of the Brainomix software, to be used in the NHS while more evidence is gathered. NICE stated that it is unclear how much of the faster access to treatment comes from the software. In January 2026 researchers at the University of Rzeszow in Poland, with no tie to Brainomix, reported that the software found 83.5% of anterior large vessel occlusions in 109 past transfers, and they estimated a median saving of up to 30 minutes in door-in-door-out time.
